Topic 01 — CV Adaptations · 1 of 5

↑ Maximal Cardiac Output

The Most Significant Change
Most significant CV change with 6–12 months aerobic endurance training: ↑ maximal cardiac output.
Primary driver ↑ Stroke volume → ↑ LV chamber volume (more blood) + ↑ contractility (stronger ejection).
Maximal HR Generally unaltered/slight ↓ with prolonged training — due to ↑ parasympathetic tone.
LV Remodelling
Aerobic training → volume overload pattern (contrast with RT pressure overload):
↑ LV chamber volume (end-diastolic volume) — more blood per beat
↑ LV wall thickness (modest) — to accommodate larger chamber
↑ LV contractility — stronger ejection at rest/exercise
Result Resting SV: ≈79→≈76 mL (minor ↑) untrained; elite male: ≈147 mL.
Aerobic training→↑ LV chamber volume + contractility→↑ Stroke volume→↑ Max cardiac output→↑ VO₂max
Source: my.clevelandclinic.org
Topic 01 — CV Adaptations · 2 of 5

Resting Bradycardia & HR Response

Resting Bradycardia
Aerobic endurance training ↓ resting HR — hallmark adaptation: bradycardia.
SA node discharge Normal: 60–80 bpm. Aerobic training → ↓ discharge rate via ↑ parasympathetic tone.
↑ Stroke volume effect ↑ Blood/contraction → heart contracts less often for same CO → ↓ resting HR.
Elite aerobic endurance athletes Resting HR: 40–60 bpm. Untrained 76.4 → trained 57.0 bpm.
HR During Exercise
Submaximal exercise: ↓ HR at any given workload — hallmark of aerobic fitness.
HR ↑ more slowly in trained vs sedentary, same workload.
Maximal exercise HR Unchanged or slight ↓ with prolonged training.
HR recovery Trained athletes recover HR faster post-exercise — a key marker for monitoring readiness.
Key figures: Untrained resting HR: 76.4 → 57.0 bpm after training. Elite male: 45 bpm · Elite female: 51 bpm. Maximal HR: 192.8 → 190.8 (minimal change). ↓ Submaximal HR for same work = direct measure of cardiorespiratory fitness.
Topic 01 — CV Adaptations · 3 of 5

↑ Capillary Density & Blood Volume

Capillary Density
↑ Capillary density with aerobic endurance training — depends on training volume + intensity.
What capillaries do Deliver O₂, nutrients, hormones. Remove heat + metabolic by-products (CO₂, lactate, H⁺). ↑ density = ↓ diffusion distance = faster exchange.
Key data Capillary number/mm²: 289 → 356 (untrained to trained). Number/fiber: 1.39 → 1.95. Elite: 2.15 capillaries/fiber.
Consequence ↑ Capillarisation + ↑ mitochondrial density → improved a-vO₂ difference → ↑ VO₂max.
Blood Volume
Aerobic training → ↑ blood (plasma) volume — supports ↑ SV + cardiac output.
Plasma volume ↑ ↑ Plasma volume → ↑ total blood volume → ↑ SV at max exercise.
Hemoglobin mass ↑ ↑ Total Hb mass. Hematocrit %: slight ↓ — dilutional effect (plasma volume ↑ more than Hb mass).
Net effect ↑ O₂-carrying capacity + ↓ blood viscosity → ↑ cardiac output efficiency.
a-vO₂ difference: VO₂max = max cardiac output × a-vO₂ difference. Aerobic training ↑ both: ↑ O₂ delivery (↑ CO) + ↑ O₂ extraction (↑ a-vO₂ diff) → multiplicative ↑ VO₂max.
Source: mylwi.com
Topic 01 — CV Adaptations · 4 of 5

VO₂max — Criterion Index of CV Fitness

What VO₂max Is
Most significant measurable adaptation to aerobic endurance training. Criterion index of CV fitness.
Formula VO₂max = Max cardiac output × Arteriovenous O₂ difference
Determined by Genetics + training program. ↑ Intensity → ↑ O₂ consumption until plateau → VO₂max reached despite continued effort.
Key data Untrained: 36.0 → 48.0 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹. Elite male: 90.6 · Elite female: 72.8 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹.
Interval training: Short high-intensity interval sprints ↑ maximal oxygen uptake if rest periods also short. Repeated sprint-sequence session = ≥2 bouts ≥10 seconds, recovery ≤60 seconds. Longer rest: ↑ sprint speed, not maximal aerobic power.
Source: trackcyclingacademy.com
Topic 01 — CV Adaptations · 5 of 5

Lactate Threshold & OBLA

Critical Power & OBLA
Critical power = athlete's maximal oxidative energy capacity. Rate of lactate production = rate of clearance by muscles + other tissues.
OBLA (Onset of Blood Lactate Accumulation) Occurs at higher %VO₂max in trained: up to 80–90% vs ≈50–60% untrained.
Why it matters Aerobic training ↑ absolute lactate threshold → athlete works at higher relative/absolute %VO₂max before lactate accumulates.
Performance Impact
Two athletes, same VO₂max (e.g. 50 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹), can perform very differently — depends on lactate threshold:
Athlete A — 80% threshold Threshold at 40 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹ → maintains 5 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹ higher power output than Athlete B.
Athlete B — 70% threshold Threshold at 35 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹ → slower race pace despite identical VO₂max.
Practical outcomes ↑ %VO₂max race pace · ↑ second-half recovery · ↑ sustained intensity throughout event.

In experienced athletes (VO₂max plateaued): lactate threshold + exercise economy = primary performance differentiators.

Source: link.springer.com
Topic 01 — CV Adaptations · Exercise Economy

Exercise Economy

What It Is
Exercise economy = energy cost per unit work/movement at given speed/power. Driven mainly by biomechanics + technique; influenced by metabolic, cardiovascular, neuromuscular efficiency.
Why it matters Two athletes, identical VO₂max + lactate threshold, can have different race outcomes. Better economy = faster pace, same energy cost.
What Improves It
Neural adaptations ↑ Motor recruitment efficiency, ↓ muscle activity variability between strides/pedal strokes
Elastic energy storage ↑ Muscle coactivation → ↑ eccentric-to-concentric ratio → ↑ use of stored elastic energy → ↓ metabolic cost
Substrate efficiency ↑ Fat oxidation → glycogen sparing → prolonged high-intensity performance
Technique refinement ↓ Muscle activity per unit work; shorter activation durations in trained cyclists/runners
Body fat & economy: Aerobic endurance training ↓ % body fat. For sports moving body mass (running): ↓ fat mass = ↓ metabolic cost/stride = ↑ economy. Excessive training + inadequate nutrition → catabolic dominance → ↓ recovery/performance.

Respiratory
Adaptations

Source: theory.labster.com
Topic 02 — Respiratory Adaptations

Does the Lung Limit Performance?

General Rule
Pulmonary ventilation generally does not limit aerobic exercise — respiratory system handles high-intensity aerobic demands for most athletes.
Unaffected or moderately affected Aerobic training leaves respiratory system unaffected/moderately changed.
Exception — elite highly trained athletes In some highly trained athletes: total body aerobic exercise may exceed respiratory functional capacity → affects O₂ transport to locomotor muscle.
Training Adaptations Include
↑ Tidal volume Air volume/breath ↑ with maximal exercise.
↑ Breathing frequency ↑ With maximal exercise demand.
Submaximal shift Submaximal: breathing frequency often ↓, tidal volume ↑ — more air/breath, fewer breaths needed.
Key data Maximal pulmonary ventilation: 128.7 → 156.4 L/min (untrained to trained). Elite male: 164.4 L/min.
Ventilatory adaptations result from local/neural/chemical changes in specific trained muscles — highly specific to exercise type, not generalisable across activities.
Topic 02 — Respiratory Adaptations · Specificity

Ventilatory Specificity

Specificity Rule
Ventilatory adaptations during lower extremity exercise mainly result from lower extremity training.
Key implication Lower extremity training (e.g. running, cycling) → ↓ lactate + CO₂ production from buffering in those muscles — but produces no ventilatory adaptation for upper extremity activities (untrained there).
Maximal vs Submaximal
Maximal exercise ↑ Tidal volume + ↑ breathing frequency — both ↑ to meet max ventilatory demand.
Submaximal exercise ↓ Breathing frequency + ↑ tidal volume — more efficient gas exchange/breath. Trained athletes breathe slower at same workload vs untrained.
Resting ventilation Resting: 10.9 → 12.0 L/min (minimal change). Elite male: 11.8 L/min. Adaptation is mainly in exercise response, not rest.
!
Practical implication for S&C professionals: A runner with excellent respiratory efficiency won't automatically show the same ventilatory adaptations in swimming/upper-body ergometry. Sport-specific aerobic conditioning must match the sport's actual movement patterns.
Topic 03

Neural
Adaptations

Topic 03 — Neural Adaptations

Movement Economy & Neuromuscular Efficiency

Understudied but Important
Neural adaptations from chronic aerobic training are relatively understudied vs strength/power training. Clear adaptations still occur — particularly in movement economy.
Key adaptations ↑ Movement economy via motor recruitment patterns. ↑ Muscle coactivation. ↑ Leg stiffness. ↑ Eccentric-to-concentric ratio.
Net effect ↑ Elastic energy storage/use → ↓ metabolic cost of exercise.
Evidence in Cyclists & Runners
Trained cyclists/runners: ↓ variability in muscle activity between pedal strokes/strides vs novices.
Shorter muscle activation duration ↓ Muscle activity per unit movement — more precisely timed, economical contractions.
Triathletes (multisport interference) Triathletes show more extensive, variable muscle coactivation, less refined patterns in cycling/running vs single-sport athletes — reflects neuromuscular interference from multisport training.
Chronic aerobic training→↑ Motor recruitment precision→↑ Eccentric-to-concentric ratio→↑ Elastic energy use→↓ Metabolic cost = ↑ Economy
Source: mdpi.com
Topic 03 — Neural Adaptations · Elastic Energy

Leg Stiffness & Elastic Energy

Muscle Coactivation ↑
Chronic aerobic training → ↑ muscle coactivation (simultaneous activation of agonist + antagonist muscle groups around a joint).
Functional benefit ↑ Leg stiffness running → musculotendinous unit stores more elastic potential energy in eccentric (landing) phase.
Release on concentric phase Elastic energy released in propulsive phase → ↓ ATP demand for force → ↓ metabolic cost/stride.
Eccentric-to-Concentric Ratio
↑ Eccentric-to-concentric ratio enables athletes to:
Use stored elastic energy more efficiently Stretch-shortening cycle (SSC) optimised — longer pre-activation, better stiffness regulation.
Reduce metabolic cost Each stride costs less metabolically, same mechanical output — neural component of running economy gains.
Contrast with strength training RT neural adaptations: ↑ recruitment + ↑ firing rate. Aerobic: pattern refinement + energy recycling.
Multisport interference: Triathletes show more extensive/variable muscle coactivation, less modulation in cycling/running vs single-sport athletes — multisport training interferes with sport-specific neuromuscular refinement. Implications for concurrent training programme design.

Source: sciencefacts.net
Topic 04 — Muscular Adaptations · 1 of 4

↑ Mitochondria & Myoglobin

Mitochondria
Aerobic training → ↑ size + number of mitochondria in trained muscle fibers.
What mitochondria do Aerobically produce ATP via oxidation of pyruvate, lactate, free fatty acids. Larger/more mitochondria = ↑ capacity to extract/use O₂.
Key data Succinate dehydrogenase (SDH) activity: 6.4 → 17.7 μmol·g⁻¹·min⁻¹ (nearly 3× increase). Elite: 21.6 μmol·g⁻¹·min⁻¹. Citrate synthase: 35.9 → 45.1 μmol·min⁻¹·g⁻¹.
Mitochondrial density ↑ Unlike RT (CSA ↑ dilutes density), aerobic training directly ↑ both number + density.
Myoglobin
Myoglobin = protein transporting oxygen within the cell (intracellular O₂ store/shuttle).
Aerobic training → ↑ myoglobin content Combined with ↑/larger mitochondria → greatly ↑ muscle O₂ extraction/use capacity.
Triple synergy ↑ Capillary density (O₂ delivery) + ↑ myoglobin (O₂ transport within cell) + ↑ mitochondria (O₂ utilisation) = multiplicative ↑ muscle aerobic capacity.
Contrast with RT RT: ↑ CSA, ↓ mitochondrial density (diluted). Aerobic: no major CSA gain, large ↑ mitochondrial content.
Topic 04 — Muscular Adaptations · 2 & 3 of 4

Oxidative Enzymes & Glycogen Sparing

↑ Oxidative Enzyme Activity
Aerobic training → ↑ levels/activity of oxidative metabolism enzymes — biochemical infrastructure for aerobic energy production.
Citrate synthase Krebs cycle rate-limiting enzyme. 35.9 → 45.1 μmol·min⁻¹·g⁻¹.
Succinate dehydrogenase (SDH) Krebs cycle + electron transport chain marker. 6.4 → 17.7 (↑ 177%). Elite: 21.6.
Lactate dehydrogenase Variable response — may ↓ (less glycolysis reliance).
Fat-metabolising enzymes ↑ activity → ↑ ability to oxidise free fatty acids → ↑ fat use during exercise.
Also worth noting: Aerobic training spares muscle glycogen (less use during exercise) + ↑ fat use within muscle — both via ↑ fat-metabolising enzymes + ↑ mitochondrial respiratory capacity. Prolongs performance at same intensity.
Topic 04 — Muscular Adaptations · 4 of 4

Fiber Type Transitions

IIx → IIa Transition
Little evidence of Type II → Type I conversion with aerobic training. May be gradual conversion within Type II subgroups: IIx → IIa.
Why significant Type IIa: ↑ oxidative capacity vs IIx — functionally closer to Type I. Shift → more aerobically efficient muscle.
Key data % Type I fibers: 48% → 51% (untrained before → after). Elite male: 60.8%. Elite female: 60.4–61.8%. Aerobic training → ↑ oxidative phenotype of muscle.
Hybrid Fibers & Fiber Size
Hybrid fibers = fibers with combo of two/three MHC isoforms (pure + mixed). Can ↑/↓ depending on muscle composition + exercise stimulus.
Marathon training study (Trappe et al.) 16-week marathon training (+3-week taper): ≈50% ↓ hybrid fiber %. ↑ Type I fibers in gastrocnemius — volume-adjusted, influenced by training volume.
Fiber size — unexpected finding 13 weeks marathon training → ↓20% fiber size (Type I/II) — strength maintained, Type IIa strength even ↑18% after 3-week taper. Smaller fibers → shorter O₂ diffusion distance → ↑ aerobic efficiency.
Relative ↑ in aerobic potential similar in Type I/II fibers with endurance training — but Type I's higher initial aerobic capacity keeps its absolute capacity greater before/after training.
Source: muscleandfitness.com
Topic 04 — Muscular Adaptations · Body Composition

Body Composition & Protein Turnover

Body Composition
Aerobic endurance training generally → ↓ relative % body fat — assuming appropriate nutrition.
Fat-free mass Little/no effect on fat-free mass. Contrast: RT ↑ fat-free mass.
Longer programs Greater ↓ % body fat with longer-term programs.
Caution Excessive training → catabolic dominance → catabolic/anabolic imbalance → ↓ performance + health.
Protein Turnover
Aerobic training (esp. running) often → acute ↑ net protein breakdown from muscle — cortisol-driven.
Despite anabolic hormones Despite ↑ testosterone + IGF-1, net protein synthesis in skeletal muscle is mainly mitochondrial, not contractile.
Recovery nutrition Post-exercise nutrition (protein + carbs) critical — mitochondrial/myofibrillar turnover rates differ; timing influences pathway priority.
RED-S (Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport): Low energy availability affects protein involvement in aerobic endurance exercise, esp. long-duration bouts. Training variables + energy supply need management across a season. See Chapter 11.

Bone &
Connective
Tissue

Topic 05 — Bone & Connective Tissue

Bone Adaptation is Activity-Specific

Running — High Impact
Running promotes bone growth more than most aerobic exercise — via repetitive high-impact loading (forces several × body weight).
Runners vs controls Runners: ↑ total/leg bone mineral density vs non-exercising controls.
Runners vs cyclists Runners: ↑ total/leg BMD vs cyclists too (cyclists: ↓ lower spine BMD vs controls).
Key principle: Skeletal adaptations to aerobic endurance training are specific to the activity — specifically its axial loading. Bone responds to load magnitude + rate, not just aerobic demand.
Topic 05 — Bone & Connective Tissue · Bone Growth Principles

Stimulating Bone Growth via Aerobic Exercise

1
Exceed MES and strain frequency: Activity must exceed daily intensity threshold + cyclical strain frequency to drive bone growth. Progressive overload applies to bone as to muscle.
2
↑ Rate of limb movement: Bone responds to load magnitude + rate. HIIT → greater osteogenic stimulus + aerobic training benefits.
3
Concurrent training for bone: Aerobic + resistance training = known stimulus for ↑ bone mass — strongest osteogenic combo. RT provides high mechanical loads aerobic often can't.
4
Oxygen transport limitation: Further bone overload via aerobic exercise is eventually limited by O₂ transport system (not musculoskeletal limits). RT must then supplement for bone benefit.
High-impact cyclical loading: Gymnastics, volleyball, basketball → selectively ↑ BMD at hip + spine. Repeated high forces — more osteogenic than low-impact continuous activity, even at same aerobic intensity.
Topic 05 — Bone & Connective Tissue · Soft Tissues

Tendons, Ligaments & Cartilage

Tendons & Ligaments
In mature adults, tendon/ligament growth + strength are proportional to exercise stimulus intensity, especially weight-bearing activities.
Structural adaptation Collagen fibers ↑ in number, size, density with consistent exercise stimulation.
Threshold requirement Exercise intensity must exceed daily-activity strain on connective tissues to drive change. Low-intensity aerobic exercise may be insufficient.
Key data Ligament strength: ↑. Tendon strength: ↑. Collagen content: Variable.
Cartilage
Weight-bearing activity benefits cartilage — in the knee joint, weight-bearing surfaces are thicker than non-weight-bearing surfaces.
Complete ROM essential Full ROM during weight bearing likely essential for tissue viability — ensures synovial fluid circulation + nutrient delivery.
Running & knee OA debate Study of thousands of non-elite runners (ages 12–50): running did not increase odds of knee pain or symptomatic knee OA. May even offer protection via ↑ periarticular strength + proprioception.
Elite aerobic athletes & OA: Former power/mixed-sport athletes (soccer, basketball, track): ↑ premature OA admission rates vs aerobic endurance athletes (long-distance runners), who showed admissions at a notably older age. Lower BMI + active lifestyle may protect.
Source: cjdonline.com
Topic 05 — Bone & Connective Tissue · Running & Joints

Running & Knee Osteoarthritis — The Evidence

Concern (Historic View)
Habitual running suggested to harm joints (knees, hips) — ↑ risk of cartilage damage/OA via repetitive impact loading.
Current Evidence
Running does not increase odds of knee pain or symptomatic knee OA in non-elite runners — no ↑ risk vs non-running activities.
Possible Protection
Some research: running may even protect against general knee pain — linked to ↑ periarticular strength + proprioception from running motion.
Elite Athlete Caveat
Exposure level (duration, intensity, frequency) may be a risk factor for knee OA in elites. Power/mixed-sport athletes show earlier onset OA than aerobic endurance athletes.
Protective mechanisms in aerobic endurance athletes: Lower BMI helps prevent OA. More active lifestyle → above-average life expectancy → later OA onset if it occurs. No notable differences between elite/non-elite running athletes.
Topic 06

Endocrine
Adaptations

Topic 06 — Endocrine Adaptations

Hormonal Response — Maximal vs Submaximal

Maximal Exercise
High-intensity aerobic training ↑ absolute secretion rates of many hormones at maximal exercise.
Why ↑ Hormonal response at maximal exercise helps athlete tolerate/sustain prolonged high-intensity exercise.
Fight-or-flight (very short, very high) Very high intensity + very short duration (5–10 s) → only fight-or-flight hormone changes: ↑ epinephrine + norepinephrine.
Key to endocrine responses in aerobic athletes: Interaction between training variables (volume + intensity + duration) + energy supply determines endocrine response + adaptations during/after training.
Source: chappo-healthnutrition.com
Topic 06 — Endocrine Adaptations · Energy Availability

Energy Availability & RED-S

Low Energy Availability Effects
Low energy availability affects protein involvement in aerobic endurance exercise, especially long-duration bouts.
Testosterone ↓ Athletes running greater mileage with low energy availability: ↓ basal testosterone.
Hormonal sensitivity Testosterone + insulin more sensitive to energy availability/training load changes than cortisol/GH — useful monitoring markers.
Protein catabolism ↑ Low energy → greater reliance on protein as fuel → accelerated muscle breakdown + impaired adaptation.
RED-S (Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport)
RED-S = impaired physiological function from relative energy deficiency — affects endocrine, metabolic, haematological, immunological, psychological + bone health systems.
Athletes at risk Endurance athletes with high training volumes + inadequate energy intake: particular risk. Formerly "Female Athlete Triad" — now recognised to affect all athletes regardless of sex.
Endocrine impact ↓ Testosterone · ↓ estrogen · ↓ IGF-1 · ↑ cortisol → bone loss, impaired muscle adaptation, hormonal suppression + impaired recovery.
See Chapter 11 Full detail on RED-S management + nutritional strategies.
Recovery nutrition is critical: Post-exercise nutrition (protein + carbs) essential for aerobic endurance athletes. Mitochondrial/myofibrillar turnover rates differ — timing may favor one pathway. Early post-exercise nutrition especially important during high-volume training.
Topic 06 — Endocrine Adaptations · Protein Pathways

Protein Pathways in Aerobic Athletes

1
Acute protein breakdown: Aerobic exercise (esp. running) → acute ↑ net protein breakdown from muscle — cortisol-driven (stress), despite concurrent ↑ anabolic hormones (testosterone, IGF-1).
2
Mitochondrial vs contractile protein synthesis: Net protein synthesis in skeletal muscle of aerobic athletes occurs — mainly mitochondrial, not contractile (actin/myosin). RT: contractile synthesis dominates.
3
Differential turnover rates: Mitochondrial/myofibrillar turnover rates may differ — influences post-exercise recovery capacity. Protein ingestion may shift pathway priority (mitochondrial vs myofibrillar).
4
Session intensity interacts with recovery: High/low-intensity sessions may alter protein pathway preference. Exercise-nutrient interaction at different intensities: still evolving research — early post-exercise protein + carb remains the consistent recommendation.
5
Muscle hypertrophy in aerobic athletes: Possible — mainly from mitochondrial protein accumulation, not myofibrillar addition. Explains why aerobic endurance athletes show well-developed oxidative capacity without RT-like CSA gains.
Aerobic exercise→↑ Cortisol (acute)→↑ Protein breakdown+↑ Anabolic hormones→Net: ↑ mitochondrial protein synthesis

Topic 07 — External Factors · 1 of 6

Altitude — Acute & Chronic Responses

Acute Responses (≥3,900 ft / 1,189 m)
Immediate adjustments to compensate for ↓ partial pressure of O₂:
① Hyperventilation ↑ breathing frequency (primarily); ventilation stabilises with time
② ↑ Submaximal cardiac output due primarily to ↑ HR (30–50% above sea-level values)
③ Stroke volume constant/slight ↓
④ ↓ Arterial O₂ saturation → ↓ VO₂max + ↓ aerobic performance
⑤ Body fluids more alkaline due to ↓ CO₂ with hyperventilation
Chronic Acclimatization
Within 10–14 days: HR + cardiac output return toward normal via longer-term acclimatization — ↑ red blood cell production (polycythemia):
↑ Hemoglobin (5–15%; up to 30–50% RBC ↑)
↑ Diffusing capacity of O₂ through pulmonary membranes
↑ Capillarisation + ↑ mitochondria in skeletal muscle
↑ Fat use, sparing glycogen
Acid-base balance maintenance via renal HCO₃⁻ excretion + hyperventilation
Minimum 3–6 weeks needed to adapt at moderate altitude (2,200–3,000 ft / 608–914 m)
Altitude mechanism chain: ↓ Ambient O₂ → ↓ arterial O₂ content → ↑ HIF-α stabilisation → ↑ EPO → ↑ Hb mass + RBC volume → ↑ a-vO₂ differential → ↑ VO₂max → ↑ aerobic endurance performance. Acclimatization reverts ≈one month after return to sea level.
Source: altitudecentre.com
Topic 07 — External Factors · 2 of 6

Heat Acclimatization

Key Chronic Adaptations
Repeated exposure to hot environment → thermoregulatory + physiological adaptations:
Earlier onset of sweating + ↑ sweat rate + ↑ evaporative cooling
↓ Resting + exercising skin + core body temperature
↑ Plasma volume (sudden, large expansion) → ↑ blood volume → ↑ SV → ↑ VO₂max
↓ Resting + exercising HR
↑ Myocardial protection + ↑ heat shock proteins
↓ Gastrointestinal distress
Timeline & Decay
Adaptations start from first day of exposure. ~75% of adaptations occur within first 4–6 days.
Decay rate For every day without heat exposure: 2.5% loss of adaptations. Full loss expected after ~1 month without repeated heat stress.
Aerobic fitness advantage Higher aerobic fitness → ↑ ability to exercise in heat + better retention of heat adaptations.
Sex differences Females: greater ↑ body temp in heat (lower thermosensitivity + sweat rate) → may need slightly longer protocol for thermoregulatory stability.
Heat mechanism chain: ↑ Core body temperature → ↑ heat shock proteins → ↑ HIF-α stabilisation → ↑ aldosterone → ↑ plasma volume → ↑ SV + → ↑ VO₂max + ↑ lactate threshold → ↑ aerobic endurance performance. Also: ↑ VEGF → ↑ skeletal muscle blood flow.
Source: trainright.com
Topic 07 — External Factors · 3 & 4 of 6

Hyperoxic Breathing · Smoking & Vaping

Hyperoxic Breathing
Breathing O₂-enriched gas during rest/post-exercise → short-term improvements:
↑ O₂ transport · ↑ Lactate metabolism · ↑ Power output · ↑ Work tolerance vs normoxic breathing
Long-term supplementation Systematic long-term supplementation during endurance training shows contradictory results, small overall benefit. Normal sea-level breathing: 95–98% arterial Hb O₂ saturation — already near maximum. Full potential of hyperoxic breathing still unclear.
Smoking & Vaping
Both impair aerobic exercise performance:
Smoking — key mechanisms ① ↑ Airway resistance (bronchiole constriction). ② Paralysis of cilia → debris accumulation. ③ Carboxyhemoglobin (CO binds Hb > O₂) → ↓ O₂ carrying capacity → ↑ submaximal CV responses.
Vaping Most common nicotine modality in young people (27.5% US high school students in 2019). Regular vaping → ↓ VO₂peak. Short-term: ↑ HR + diastolic BP via catecholamine release. Lung inflammation + cellular damage → ↓ lung capacity + impaired gas exchange. Long-term CV changes (heart failure risk).
Vaping vs smoking: Vaping users: significantly slower 2-mile run times than non-vapers — even slower than traditional smokers in some studies. ↓ O₂ extraction, ↓ chronotropic response, ↓ VO₂peak even in young healthy regular vapers.
Source: storymd.com
Topic 07 — External Factors · 5 & 6 of 6

Blood Doping & Genetic Potential

Blood Doping
Artificially ↑ red blood cell mass via:
RBC infusion (own or donor) — rapid ↑ for a few weeks
EPO administration — slower ↑ but sustained as long as EPO is given
Both → ↑ O₂ carrying capacity → ↑ O₂ to working muscles → ↑ VO₂max up to 11%. At submaximal workloads: ↓ HR, ↓ blood lactate, ↑ pH.
Health risks ↑ Hematocrit → ↑ blood viscosity → risk of stroke, MI, DVT, pulmonary embolism. ↑ Arterial BP. Flu-like symptoms. Risks from transfusion/infusion.
Genetic Potential
Upper limit of individual genetic potential significantly shapes absolute magnitude of training adaptations.
System-level ceiling Each biological system (e.g. cardiovascular) has an upper adaptation limit. Closer to limit → smaller gains per unit training.
Elite performance implications In elite competitions (e.g. swimming): small gains = difference between gold and 26th place. Where tenths/hundredths of a second matter, 0.05% improvement may justify major training investment.
Program design + monitoring Near genetic ceiling: careful program design + monitoring critical to extract remaining small gains.
Blood doping + altitude interaction: ↑ Altitude → ↓ blood doping's added benefit — bone marrow already maximally stimulated by hypoxia. Blood doping benefits mainly those already heat-acclimatized; little aid for non-acclimatized individuals in heat.
Topic 08

Detraining

Topic 08 — Detraining

Detraining vs Tapering

Detraining
Detraining = partial/complete loss of training-induced adaptations from insufficient training stimulus.
Governed by Principle of training reversibility — adaptations are transient, disappear when training load is insufficient/removed.
Results in Partial/complete reversal of adaptations → ↓ athletic performance. Aerobic endurance adaptations most sensitive to inactivity due to enzymatic basis.
Prevention Proper exercise variation, intensity, maintenance programs + active recovery periods can adequately protect against serious detraining effects.
Tapering (NOT Detraining)
Tapering = planned reduction in training volume (duration + frequency but not intensity) before competition or planned recovery microcycle.
Purpose Designed to enhance athletic performance + adaptations — allows accumulated fatigue to dissipate while maintaining fitness.
Key distinction Intensity maintained during tapering → neuromuscular + metabolic adaptations preserved. ↓ Volume allows residual fatigue to clear → often performance peaks.
Marathon study example After 13 weeks marathon training (↓ fiber size 20%), 3-week taper → ↑ Type IIa fiber strength 18% — demonstrates performance benefit of planned volume reduction.
Topic 08 — Detraining · VO₂max Loss

VO₂max Loss — Timeline

Short-Term
< 4 weeks
↓ 4–14% VO₂max (Highly Trained Athletes)
Mainly from ↓ blood volume → ↓ stroke volume → ↓ max cardiac output + ↑ submaximal HR. CV changes are the primary early driver of VO₂max loss — not enzymatic changes.
Long-Term
> 4 weeks
↓ 6–20% VO₂max (Highly Trained Athletes)
From ↓ blood volume → ↓ stroke volume → ↓ max cardiac output + ↑ submaximal HR. Enzymatic changes now also contribute — ↓ oxidative enzyme activity + ↓ mitochondrial density. Aerobic endurance performance loss tracks VO₂max loss.
Key references: Two review articles address factors contributing to aerobic performance — most importantly VO₂max (cardiac output + a-vO₂ difference) — and impact of short-term (<4 weeks)/long-term (>4 weeks) detraining. Highly trained athletes: short-term ↓ 4–14%; long-term ↓ 6–20%.
Topic 08 — Detraining · Enzymatic Basis

Enzymatic Sensitivity & Prevention

Why Aerobic Adaptations Are Most Sensitive
Aerobic endurance adaptations are most sensitive to inactivity due to enzymatic basis — oxidative enzymes rapidly lose activity without sustained training stimulus.
Exact mechanisms unknown Cellular mechanisms dictating detraining changes are unknown; further research needed. Known: enzyme activity + mitochondrial density highly labile.
Contrast with resistance training Strength detraining is slower, less pronounced — structural changes (CSA) persist longer than aerobic fitness's biochemical infrastructure.
Prevention Strategies
Exercise variation Varying training modalities maintains stimulus across different muscle groups + metabolic pathways — reduces risk of staleness + provides continued stimulus for enzymatic maintenance.
Maintain intensity During reduced training (e.g. tapering, travel, off-season): maintaining intensity while ↓ volume preserves aerobic adaptations far longer than ↓ intensity.
Active recovery periods Even low-intensity activity during planned recovery maintains minimum enzymatic + cardiovascular adaptations.
Maintenance programs Reduced-frequency maintenance programs (even 1–2×/week high-intensity sessions) can preserve VO₂max adaptations for extended periods.

Proper exercise variation, intensity maintenance, and active recovery can adequately protect against serious detraining effects.
